title: 4. Kappa architecture
summary: One streaming path over a replayable log: reprocessing by replay, Kafka retention and tiered storage, and the workloads where a single stream path struggles.

blocks.text: 40.1 Context and the problem it solved

Teams running Lambda were maintaining the same business logic twice, in Storm and in Hadoop, and spending much of their time reconciling the two. At LinkedIn, Kafka was already a durable, ordered, partitioned log, and Samza processed it with local state. In 2014 Jay Kreps proposed Kappa; his observation was that the only thing the batch layer really provided was **reprocessing**: rerunning logic over full history after a code change or bug. A log with long retention can provide that too.

items: **One code base**: the same job serves both live processing and backfills.
**One set of infrastructure**: a log plus a stream processor plus a serving store.
**Reprocessing on demand**: start a new consumer from offset zero (or from a timestamp) and build a new output table in parallel.

blocks.text: 40.2 Reference diagram

blocks.title: Kappa architecture
blocks.caption: There is no batch layer. History lives in the log, not in a separate master dataset.

blocks.text: All input lands in log topics, keyed and partitioned. A stream job consumes them, keeps state (windows, joins, aggregates) in a fault-tolerant state backend, and writes results to a serving store. Consumers read only the serving store.
Reprocessing by replay

items: Deploy job v2 with a new consumer group, starting from the earliest retained offset.
v2 writes to a new output table (for example `orders_agg_v2`) while v1 keeps serving.
Monitor v2's consumer lag; when it catches up to the head of the log, compare v1 and v2 outputs.
Switch readers to v2 (rename, view swap or config change).
Stop v1 and drop its table.

blocks.text: Replay throughput is the key number. A job that normally handles 5,000 events per second at the head may need to replay 30 days, roughly 13 billion events. At 200,000 events per second with extra parallelism, that is about 18 hours. Plan reprocessing capacity explicitly; it is the Kappa equivalent of a batch window.
40.3 Components and technology choices

head: Layer
Component
Typical tools
rows: Apache Kafka, Redpanda, Amazon Kinesis (shorter retention), Apache Pulsar
Kafka tiered storage, Confluent Infinite Storage, Pulsar offloading, Redpanda tiered storage
Apache Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming
Druid, Pinot, ClickHouse, Cassandra, Elasticsearch, Iceberg tables

blocks.text: **Retention** decides what can be replayed. Kafka retains by time (`retention.ms`) or size per topic, and `-1` means keep forever. Keeping months of data on broker disks is expensive, so **tiered storage** offloads closed log segments to object storage while brokers keep only a recent hot set. Consumers reading old offsets fetch from the object store transparently, at lower throughput than local disk. Exact behaviour and limits differ by version and vendor; check the current documentation.

**Compacted topics** (`cleanup.policy=compact`) keep only the latest value per key. They are ideal for replaying current state such as a customer table, but they lose the history of changes, so they cannot rebuild an SCD type 2 dimension.

blocks.title: Topic with infinite retention, and one with compaction (Kafka CLI)
blocks.text:
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker:9092 --create \
  --topic orders.events --partitions 24 --replication-factor 3 \
  --config retention.ms=-1

kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker:9092 --create \
  --topic customers.current --partitions 12 --replication-factor 3 \
  --config cleanup.policy=compact

**Where Iceberg, Snowflake and semantic models fit.** Iceberg is increasingly the Kappa archive and serving sink: Flink writes Iceberg tables continuously, and some streaming platforms can expose topics as Iceberg tables, which turns the log's history into queryable files (chapter 45). Snowflake fits as a downstream consumer through Snowpipe Streaming or the Kafka connector, not as part of the processing path. A semantic model sits on the serving tables; Kappa itself does not provide one.
40.4 Modelling and data layers in this architecture

head: Layer
Kappa form
Design rule
rows: Immutable, long or infinite retention; this is the replay source
Stable keys and schemas; can be rebuilt by replay, so shorter retention is acceptable
Idempotent upserts by key so replay overwrites rather than duplicates
Join with temporal semantics to get the value valid at event time

blocks.text: Modelling in Kappa is mostly about **keys, event time and idempotency**. Every output must be safe to rebuild: if job v2 replays a year of data, the sink must accept upserts by primary key or be written to a fresh table. Joining facts to dimensions needs temporal joins (Flink's `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF`), otherwise a replay joins old orders to today's customer attributes and history is silently rewritten.

Replaying from the log does not reproduce the past if the job calls external services (a currency API, a lookup database) whose answers have changed since. Put that reference data in the log too, as versioned events, so that replay is deterministic.
40.5 Ingestion, orchestration and serving

Ingestion is push-based: applications produce events, and databases are captured with CDC into topics (chapter 17). There is little scheduling; **orchestration becomes deployment**. Jobs run continuously on Kubernetes or a managed Flink service, upgraded from savepoints. A DAG scheduler is still useful for reprocessing runs, compaction of sink tables, and periodic quality checks.

Serving stores must handle continuous upserts and fast reads: Pinot, Druid or ClickHouse for analytical queries, Cassandra or Redis for key lookups, Iceberg tables for broader SQL access at minute-level freshness. Monitoring centres on **consumer lag** (how far behind the head each job is), checkpoint duration and state size.
40.6 Strengths, weaknesses and failure modes

head: Strengths
Weaknesses
Typical failure modes
rows: Single code path; no batch/speed drift
Replay of long history can take hours or days
Bug found, replay estimated at 4 days, business cannot wait
Log storage for years is costly without tiering
Retention set to 7 days by default; history needed for reprocessing is gone
Complex queries over full history (ad-hoc, multi-way joins) are awkward on a log
Analysts cannot explore data, so a separate lake appears anyway
Natural fit for event-driven systems and CDC
State for large joins and long windows grows large
State backend runs out of disk; checkpoints take minutes; job restarts loop

blocks.text: Kappa struggles with workloads that are naturally **batch-shaped**: training a model over three years of data, large historical joins between unrelated datasets, ad-hoc exploration, and reports that require a fully closed period. Replaying a log to answer a question it was not designed for is slower and more expensive than scanning a well-partitioned columnar table. In practice most 'Kappa' platforms also land topics into Iceberg or a warehouse for these workloads, which edges toward the streaming lakehouse (chapters 42 and 45).
40.7 When to choose it / when not

items: **Choose it** when the main outputs are continuously updated: operational dashboards, fraud scores, inventory levels, user-facing counters.
**Choose it** when sources are already events or CDC streams and the team has streaming skills.
**Avoid it** when consumers are mainly analysts doing ad-hoc SQL over years of history.
**Avoid it** when daily or hourly freshness is enough; batch or micro-batch is simpler and cheaper.
**Avoid it** without a retention and schema-evolution plan for the raw topics.
**Combine it** with Iceberg sinks so that history is queryable as tables and the log does not need to be the only archive.

blocks.title: Logistics: shipment status in seconds
blocks.text: A parcel carrier receives 50 million scan events a day from depots and vans. Customers and call centres need current shipment status within seconds, and operations need late-delivery counts per depot per hour. The platform team built a Kappa pipeline: scans and CDC from the routing database go to Kafka with tiered storage and 13-month retention; Flink maintains per-shipment state and hourly depot aggregates.
items: Shipment status is upserted into a key-value store for the tracking API and into Iceberg for analysts.
When the definition of 'late' changed, a v2 job replayed 90 days in about 6 hours into a new table, was compared with v1, then swapped in.
Annual network planning runs as Spark over the Iceberg tables, not as a replay.

blocks.title: Size a replay
blocks.text: Your Kappa job processes payment events. Average rate is 3,000 events per second, peak 15,000. Compliance requires you to be able to recompute any output over the last 400 days. Decide retention and tiering for the raw topic, estimate how long a full replay takes at different parallelism levels, and design how v1 and v2 outputs are compared before switching. Also decide which questions you would refuse to answer by replay and send to an Iceberg table instead.
hints: Multiply rate by seconds per day by days; then divide by replay throughput.
Replay throughput from object storage may be lower than from broker disks.
Comparing outputs needs a key and a tolerance.

items: Kappa uses one streaming path; reprocessing means replaying a retained log into a new job version and output.
Retention and tiered storage determine what can be replayed and at what cost.
Compacted topics replay current state but lose change history.
Outputs must be idempotent by key, joins must be temporal, and reference data must be in the log for deterministic replay.
Kappa struggles with ad-hoc and long-history analytical workloads, so it is usually paired with Iceberg or a warehouse.

blocks.q: How does Kappa architecture handle reprocessing after a logic change?
options: It deploys a new job version that replays the retained log into a new output, then switches readers
It runs a separate nightly batch job over the data lake
It asks producers to resend their events
It edits the existing output table in place using UPDATE statements
blocks.explain: Replay from the log through a new job version is the core Kappa mechanism. A separate batch job is exactly the Lambda pattern Kappa removes.

blocks.q: Why is a compacted topic not enough to rebuild an SCD type 2 customer dimension by replay?
options: Compacted topics do not support Avro schemas
Compaction keeps only the latest value per key, so earlier versions are gone
Compacted topics cannot be read from offset zero
blocks.explain: SCD2 needs every historical version; compaction removes superseded values. Compacted topics can be read from the beginning, which is why they work well for rebuilding current state.

blocks.q: A replay of last year's orders produces different results from the original run, though the code is identical. What is a likely cause?
options: Consumer groups cannot start from earliest offsets
The job calls an external service whose answers have changed, so the enrichment is not deterministic
Tiered storage compresses old segments lossily
Kafka reorders events within a partition on replay
blocks.explain: Non-deterministic lookups break replay. Kafka preserves order within a partition, and tiered storage is lossless, so those options are wrong.

blocks.q: Which workload is the weakest fit for a pure Kappa design?
options: Real-time fraud scoring on card transactions
Ad-hoc analyst exploration joining three years of history across many datasets
blocks.explain: Long-history ad-hoc joins are batch-shaped and much cheaper on columnar tables. The other three are continuously updated outputs, which is exactly what Kappa is good at.
